bottleneck: PTSD involves fear memories that resist extinction, and reconsolidation blockade — disrupting a memory when it is recalled and labile — works in rodents but translates poorly to humans. Human traumatic memories are complex, distributed across cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus, and entangled with identity and meaning, unlike a rodent's simple fear conditioning. Propranolol administered during recall shows inconsistent effects across trials, and no method can selectively erase or rewrite one specific human memory without affecting others. The reconsolidation window in humans is poorly characterized, and recalling trauma in therapy can strengthen rather than weaken the trace.
current_state: Trauma-focused psychotherapy and EMDR help many patients but fail a substantial minority. Pharmacological memory manipulation remains experimental and unreliable, with no approved reconsolidation-blocking therapy.

title: Traumatic memories resist selective erasure
why_it_blocks: Millions live with intrusive memories that no therapy can reliably remove, and current treatments demand reliving the trauma with uncertain payoff. Cracking human reconsolidation would unlock the first direct treatment for PTSD rather than coping strategies around it.
